```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "The goal is a paying customer within 90 days, so evidence that people pay matters most. B's category has documented paying buyers: SwagUp sells $99–$999/mo tiers and Sendoso charges an estimated $15k–$20k+/yr. A's brief shows no one paying for this kind of tool beyond one listed $1.99/mo price.",
    "A faces at least four free, maintained competitors (SlopSieve, Redd-Eye, ReviewLens, ReviewGuard's free tier), several of them open source. That makes charging for a Pro tier very hard. B's competitors are priced at $99/mo and above or at enterprise levels, which leaves a plausible gap for a cheaper, Stripe-only self-serve tier.",
    "B needs only a handful of B2B buyers to hit the goal. Each early customer can be sold directly by one person. A depends on getting consumers to convert from free to paid, which needs volume, and the brief admits organic growth takes 3–6 months.",
    "B can avoid most of its operational risk by routing orders to an existing swag-fulfillment API and holding no inventory. A carries ongoing false-positive harm, DOM-scraping fragility and Reddit terms-of-service risk, with no revenue to cover maintenance.",
    "B's risks are real but named: physical logistics, customs, and PII/GDPR obligations. They limit how far B can scale more than they block a first paying customer."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's only willingness-to-pay evidence is ReviewGuard's listed $1.99/month Pro price. Nothing shows anyone actually pays it, and the brief admits no competitor publishes install or revenue numbers. Its demand quotes ('sick and tired of bots', 'take time away from reddit') show annoyance, not intent to pay, and the CEO confirmation reaches us only through a Slashdot summary of an FT report.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-low confidence. B's own demand evidence is thin: one LinkedIn comment from a gift recipient plus the seed HN quote. B's brief also notes that every competitor already offers event-triggered swag and that the category tends to sell on enterprise terms. B wins mainly because its category shows clear payment for the outcome, while A's market is dominated by free tools. Neither brief shows a specific buyer ready to pay."
}
```
